sections.title: The big question Linear Programming answers & related topics

board_events.text: Linear Programming: the best outcome from limited resources
A Diwali halwai shop makes two sweets: kaju katli and besan laddoo.
Limited khoya, limited sugar, limited hours at the stove.
How many kilos of each should I make so profit is as large as possible?
That single question IS Linear Programming.
LP = the maths of squeezing the best outcome — most profit, least cost — out of limited resources.

board_events.text: Every tool in this chapter exists to answer that one question systematically.
Three ideas do all the work
1. The objective function — the quantity you push to its best value: profit or cost.
'Linear' means $x$ and $y$ appear only to the first power — no $x^2$, no $xy$.
2. The constraints — the limits life puts on you, each a linear inequality.
Only 8 kg khoya, only 12 stove-hours, and you cannot make a negative number of laddoos.
3. The feasible region — every $(x, y)$ pair that respects all the limits at once.
Your answer is guaranteed to live inside the feasible region, or on its edge.
Why the optimum always sits at a corner
Picture the feasible region as a fenced field and $Z = ax + by$ as a ruler reading higher toward the north-east.
You want to stand where the ruler reads highest.

board_events.text: The best spot is NEVER in the open middle — it pokes out at a corner.
So you never search the whole field — you just check the corners.
Caveat 1: an unbounded field may have no maximum — you could keep walking and keep gaining.
Caveat 2: if the ruler lies parallel to a fence, a whole edge ties for best — infinitely many optima.
Caveat 3: the graphical method needs exactly two decision variables — two products, two foods.
The vocabulary examiners expect, verbatim
Objective function: the quantity being optimised, $Z = ax + by$.
Decision variables $x, y$: the quantities you choose. Constants $a, b$: profit or cost per unit.
Feasible region: the common region satisfying ALL constraints, including non-negativity $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$.
Bounded region: fits inside a circle. Unbounded region: extends to infinity in some direction.
Corner point (vertex): a point formed where two boundary lines intersect.
Feasible solution = any point in/on the region. Optimal solution = the feasible point giving the best $Z$.
Property 1: a bounded feasible region for a linear objective is a convex polygon — no dents.
Property 2: equal optimum at two corners ⇒ the same value at every point on the joining segment.

segments.text: <curious>Let me open with a question that sounds simple but is surprisingly hard to eyeball. Here is the setup.
Picture a small halwai shop in the week before Diwali. You can make two sweets, kaju katli and besan laddoo, and each earns a different profit per kilogram.
But you are short on everything that matters: only so much khoya, only so much sugar, and only so many hours at the stove before the festival rush hits.
So here is the question that keeps the shopkeeper up at night. Given everything I am short on, exactly how many kilos of each sweet should I make so that my profit is as large as possible?
That question, in one sentence, is the whole of Linear Programming.
Linear Programming is the mathematics of squeezing the best possible outcome out of limited resources, whether that means the most profit or the least cost.
Think of it as a machine. Limited inputs go in on the left, and we want the single best outcome to come out on the right.
Every tool we build in this chapter exists to answer that one question in a reliable, repeatable way.
Once you strip away the story, every Linear Programming problem is built from just three ideas. Here they are.
First, the objective function. This is the one quantity you want to push to its best value, usually your total profit that you push up, or your total cost that you push down.
We write it as Z equals a x plus b y. Z is the value we optimise, x and y are the quantities we choose, and a and b are the profit or cost per unit.
The word linear is load-bearing. It means x and y appear only to the first power. No x squared, no x times y. That straightness is exactly what makes the method work.
Second, the constraints. These are the limits life puts on you, and each one becomes a linear inequality.
For example, only eight kilograms of khoya, only twelve hours at the stove, and the obvious fact that you cannot make a negative number of laddoos.
Third, the feasible region. This is the set of every x, y pair that respects all the limits at the same time. Plot them and they fill a region of the graph.
<excited>And here is the promise that makes the whole chapter work. Your best answer is guaranteed to live inside that feasible region, or on its edge, never outside it.
Now the single most beautiful fact in this chapter, and the reason it is so easy. Let me give you the picture first.
Picture the feasible region as a fenced field. And picture the objective, Z equals a x plus b y, as a ruler whose reading climbs as you walk in one fixed direction, say towards the north-east.
Your job is simple to state. Stand at the spot in the field where the ruler reads highest.
Look at the field on the board. As we slide that ruler outward, the last point it touches before leaving the field is one of the corners.
Here is the key fact. For a straight-line ruler over a field with straight fences, the highest reading is never in the open middle of the field. It always pokes out at a corner.
That is what makes Linear Programming easy. You do not search the whole field. You just check the corners and pick the best one.
But three caveats keep you honest. First, if the field stretches off to infinity, a maximum might not exist at all, because you could keep walking north-east and keep gaining.
Second, if the ruler happens to line up parallel to one fence, then every point along that fence reads the same best value. There are then infinitely many optimal solutions.
Third, this graphical picture only works in two dimensions, that is, two decision variables. With three or more you would need algebra, the simplex method, which is beyond this chapter.
Linear Programming has no SI units and no dimensional formulae, because it is a method. So the key facts here are precise definitions, and examiners want these exact words.
The objective function is the quantity being optimised, written Z equals a x plus b y.
The decision variables x and y are the quantities you get to choose. The constants a and b are the profit or cost per unit, usually positive numbers.

The feasible region is the common region that satisfies all the constraints at once, and that includes the non-negativity conditions x greater than or equal to zero and y greater than or equal to zero.
A bounded region is one you can enclose inside a circle. An unbounded region extends to infinity in some direction.
A corner point, also called a vertex, is a point formed where two boundary lines intersect.
Keep two more straight. A feasible solution is any point inside or on the boundary of the region. An optimal solution is the feasible point that gives the best value of Z.

Now two properties worth memorising. First, a bounded feasible region for a linear objective is always a convex polygon, with no dents, so a straight line joining any two feasible points stays entirely inside.
Second, if Z takes the same optimum value at two corner points, then it takes that same value at every point on the segment joining them. That is the seed of multiple optimal solutions.

Theorem 2 — bounded vs unbounded.
If the region is BOUNDED: $Z$ has both a maximum and a minimum, each at a corner.
If the region is UNBOUNDED: a max or min may or may not exist — if it exists, still at a corner.
The unbounded case is where students lose marks — it needs a verification step.
The corner-point method, step by step
Step 1 — Draw the feasible region: turn each inequality into its boundary line and shade the correct side.
Origin test: plug in $(0, 0)$. If it satisfies the inequality, shade the origin's side.
Step 2 — Find every corner point where boundary lines cross (solve the two line equations together).
Step 3 — Evaluate $Z$ at every corner. Record the largest value $M$ and the smallest value $m$.
Step 4, bounded region: $M$ is the maximum and $m$ is the minimum. Done.
Step 4, unbounded region: you MUST verify with a half-plane test before writing the answer.
Max $M$ genuine only if $ax + by \gt M$ misses the region; min $m$ only if $ax + by \lt m$ misses it.

segments.text: The whole method rests on two theorems. C B S E states them and does not ask for a formal proof, so know them precisely, and know the procedure they justify.
Theorem one, the most important line in the chapter. When Z has an optimal value, that optimum lives at a corner.
Formally, let R be the feasible region and Z equals a x plus b y the objective. Whenever Z has an optimal value, maximum or minimum, over R, that value must occur at a corner point, a vertex of R.
The picture on the board shows why. We slide the objective line across the region, and watch where it leaves.

As you slide the line a x plus b y equals k outward, the last feasible point it touches before leaving is always a vertex, unless the line is parallel to an edge, in which case it leaves along a whole edge whose endpoints are still vertices.
Theorem two handles the shape of the region.
If the region is bounded, then Z is guaranteed to have both a maximum and a minimum, and each of them occurs at a corner point. Nothing can go wrong.
If the region is unbounded, a maximum or a minimum may or may not exist. But if it does exist, it still occurs at a corner point.
<whisper>Here is the exam secret. That unbounded case is exactly where students lose marks, because it needs an extra verification step. We build that step next.
Those two theorems justify one clean procedure, the corner-point method. Four steps, and step four has a fork.
Step one, draw the feasible region. Convert each inequality into its boundary line by replacing the inequality sign with an equals sign, plot the line, and shade the correct side.

To pick the correct side, use the origin test. Substitute the point zero, zero into the inequality. If it holds, shade the side containing the origin. If it fails, shade the other side. Use a different test point only if the line passes through the origin.
Step two, find all the corner points. These are the vertices where boundary lines cross. Read them off by inspection, or solve the two intersecting line equations simultaneously.
Step three, evaluate Z at every single corner point. Build a small table of corner point against value of Z, and mark the largest value big M and the smallest value small m.
Step four now forks on the shape. If the region is bounded, you are done. Big M is the maximum and small m is the minimum.
But if the region is unbounded, you must not stop yet. You have to verify with a half-plane test before writing any answer.

The test is this. Big M is the genuine maximum only if the open half-plane a x plus b y greater than big M has no point in common with the region. Likewise small m is the true minimum only if a x plus b y less than small m misses the region.
Let me consolidate the forms you will write again and again. Treat this section as a reference card you can jump straight to.
The heart of every problem is the objective function, Z equals a x plus b y.
First, the standard maximisation problem. This is the profit family, where your resources act as upper limits.

You write, maximise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to c one x plus d one y less than or equal to e one, c two x plus d two y less than or equal to e two, and so on, together with x and y both greater than or equal to zero.
Second, the standard minimisation problem. This is the cost family, where requirements act as lower limits.
You write, minimise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to constraints of the greater-than-or-equal type, again with x and y both greater than or equal to zero.
Now the two verification tests for unbounded regions, the lines that earn marks. For a maximum, ask whether the open half-plane beats your best corner.
If a x plus b y greater than big M shares any point with the region, then no maximum exists. Otherwise big M is the genuine maximum.
For a minimum, ask the mirror question about beating your smallest corner value.
If a x plus b y less than small m shares any point with the region, then no minimum exists. Otherwise small m is the genuine minimum.
Time to run the method on a real board-level problem. A bakery in Pune makes two kinds of cookies each morning, and we want the most profitable mix.
Each batch of nankhatai uses one kilogram of flour and three oven-slots. Each batch of kaju cookies uses two kilograms of flour and two oven-slots.
The bakery has eight kilograms of flour and twelve oven-slots. Profit is forty rupees per batch of nankhatai and fifty rupees per batch of kaju cookies.
Step one and two, formulate. Let x be batches of nankhatai and y batches of kaju. We maximise Z equals forty x plus fifty y.
The limits become x plus two y less than or equal to eight for flour, three x plus two y less than or equal to twelve for oven-slots, with x and y both non-negative.
Find where the two lines cross. Subtract the flour line from the oven line and two x equals four, so x equals two, and back-substituting gives y equals three.
Plot both lines and shade below each. The feasible region is the bounded quadrilateral O A B C you see on the board.

Now evaluate Z at every corner. At O it is zero. At A four comma zero it is one hundred sixty. At B two comma three it is eighty plus one hundred fifty, that is two hundred thirty. At C zero comma four it is two hundred.
The largest is two hundred thirty at corner B. So the bakery should bake two batches of nankhatai and three batches of kaju cookies, for a maximum profit of two hundred thirty rupees.

formally, maana R feasible region hai aur Z equals a x plus b y objective hai. Jab bhi Z ki optimal value ho, maximum ya minimum, R par, wo value zaroor kisi corner point, yaani R ke vertex par hogi.
board par picture dikhati hai kyon. hum objective line ko region ke aar-paar slide karte hain aur dekhte hain wo kahan chhodti hai.

jaise aap line a x plus b y equals k ko baahar slide karte hain, chhodne se pehle jo aakhiri feasible point chooti hai wo hamesha vertex hota hai, sivay jab line kisi edge ke parallel ho, tab wo poore edge ke saath chhodti hai jiske endpoints bhi vertices hi hain.
Theorem two region ki shape sambhalta hai.
agar region bounded hai, to Z ke paas maximum aur minimum dono hona guaranteed hai, aur har ek kisi corner point par hota hai. kuch ghalat nahi ho sakta.
agar region unbounded hai, to maximum ya minimum ho bhi sakta hai aur nahi bhi. lekin agar exist karta hai, to phir bhi kisi corner point par.
yahaan exam ka raaz hai. yahi unbounded case vo jagah hai jahaan students marks khote hain, kyunki iske liye ek extra verification step chahiye. vo step hum aage banayenge.
ye do theorems ek saaf procedure justify karte hain, corner-point method. chaar steps, aur step four mein ek fork hai.
step one, feasible region draw karein. har inequality ko uski boundary line mein badlein, yaani inequality sign ki jagah equals sign, line plot karein, aur sahi side shade karein.

sahi side chunne ke liye origin test istemal karein. point zero, zero ko inequality mein daaliye. agar sahi baithe, to origin wali side shade karein. agar nahi, to doosri side. alag test point tabhi lein jab line origin se guzarti ho.
step two, saare corner points dhoondhein. ye wo vertices hain jahan boundary lines cross karti hain. inspection se padh lein, ya dono lines ke equations ek saath solve karein.
step three, Z ko har ek corner point par evaluate karein. corner point banam Z ki value ki ek chhoti table banayein, aur sabse badi value ko big M aur sabse chhoti ko small m mark karein.
step four ab shape par fork karta hai. agar region bounded hai, to kaam khatm. big M maximum hai aur small m minimum.
lekin agar region unbounded hai, to abhi rukiye mat. answer likhne se pehle aapko half-plane test se verify karna hi hoga.

test yah hai. big M asli maximum tabhi hai jab open half-plane a x plus b y greater than big M ka region se koi common point na ho. isi tarah small m asli minimum tabhi jab a x plus b y less than small m region ko miss kar de.
jo forms aap baar-baar likhenge unhein ek jagah ikattha kar dete hain. is section ko ek reference card samjhiye jahan aap seedhe jump kar sakein.
har problem ka dil hai objective function, Z equals a x plus b y.
pehla, standard maximisation problem. yah profit family hai, jahan aapke resources upper limits ki tarah kaam karte hain.

aap likhte hain, maximise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to c one x plus d one y less than or equal to e one, c two x plus d two y less than or equal to e two, vagairah, saath mein x aur y dono greater than or equal to zero.
doosra, standard minimisation problem. yah cost family hai, jahan requirements lower limits ki tarah kaam karti hain.
aap likhte hain, minimise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to greater-than-or-equal type ki constraints, phir se x aur y dono greater than or equal to zero.
ab unbounded regions ke liye do verification tests, wo lines jo marks dilati hain. maximum ke liye puchhiye kya open half-plane aapke best corner ko beat karta hai.
agar a x plus b y greater than big M ka region se koi common point hai, to koi maximum exist nahin karta.varna big M asli maximum hai.
minimum ke liye wahi sawaal ulta poochiye, apni sabse chhoti corner value ko beat karne ke baare mein.
agar a x plus b y less than small m ka region se koi common point hai, to koi minimum exist nahi karta.varna small m asli minimum hai.
ab method ko ek asli board-level problem par chalate hain. Pune ki ek bakery har subah do tarah ki cookies banati hai, aur humein sabse profitable mix chahiye.
nankhatai ke har batch mein ek kilogram flour aur teen oven-slots lagte hain. kaju cookies ke har batch mein do kilograms flour aur do oven-slots.
bakery ke paas aath kilograms flour aur baarah oven-slots hain. profit hai chaalis rupees per batch nankhatai aur pachaas rupees per batch kaju cookies.
step one aur two, formulate karen. maana x hai nankhatai ke batches aur y hai kaju ke. hum maximise karte hain Z equals chalis x plus pachaas y.
limits ban jaati hain x plus two y less than or equal to eight flour ke liye, three x plus two y less than or equal to twelve oven-slots ke liye, saath mein x aur y dono non-negative.
dekhie dono lines kahan cross karti hain. flour line ko oven line mein se subtract karein to two x equals four, yaani x equals two, aur wapas rakhne par y equals three.
donon lines plot karein aur har ek ke neeche shade karein. feasible region wo bounded quadrilateral O A B C hai jo aap board par dekh rahe hain.

ab Z ko har corner par evaluate karein. O par zero. A yaani four comma zero par one hundred sixty. B yaani two comma three par assi plus one hundred fifty, yaani two hundred thirty. C yaani zero comma four par two hundred.
sabse badi value hai two hundred thirty, corner B par. to bakery ko do batches nankhatai aur teen batches kaju cookies banane chahiye, maximum profit two hundred thirty rupees ke liye.

board_events.text: By the multiple-optima property, every point on the segment joining them is also optimal.
So the answer is not a single corner — it is the WHOLE edge between (3, 3) and (6, 0).
Speed tip: two corner values tie ⇒ the objective line is parallel to that edge.
Worked example — dairy feed, an unbounded minimisation
Feed P ($x$ kg): 1 protein, 2 fibre. Feed Q ($y$ kg): 1 protein, 1 fibre.
Need at least 6 protein and at least 8 fibre. Cost: ₹5/kg for P, ₹4/kg for Q.

Notice what happened. The maximum value twelve is reached at two corners at once, three comma three and six comma zero.
The picture explains it. The objective line for Z equals twelve runs exactly parallel to the edge joining those two corners.

sections.title: The three questions every LPP word problem asks & related topics

board_events.text: Every word problem asks the same three questions
1. What am I choosing? → the decision variables $x$ and $y$, with units.
How many tables? how many hectares? how many scoops?
2. What am I trying to make best? → the objective $Z = ax + by$.
Total profit to push up, or total cost to push down.
3. What's stopping me? → each limit becomes a constraint, a linear inequality.
Material, money, time, demand, a promise to a customer — each is one constraint.
Factory production, diet, transport, scheduling — the same skeleton in different costumes.
Assumptions to watch — when this works, and when it bites
Proportionality: doubling production must exactly double the resource used and the profit.
A bulk discount or setup cost breaks linearity — the corner-point method no longer applies.
Divisibility: the graphical method allows fractional answers like $x = 2.5$.
CBSE problems are usually designed so the optimum lands on whole numbers.
Hidden non-negativity: buses, kilograms, hours can never be negative.
Read EVERY clause: 'type B cannot exceed type A by more than 100' is a whole constraint.
Skip one such sentence and the answer changes entirely.
The constraint-type dictionary — translate the English
'at most', 'no more than', 'cannot exceed', 'available', 'within' → upper limit → ≤
'at least', 'minimum of', 'no less than', 'requires' → lower limit → ≥
'exactly', 'must equal', 'all of it is used' → balance → =
'cannot be negative' (items, hours, kg) → non-negativity → $x, y \ge 0$
Anatomy: objective $Z = ax+by$, then structural constraints, then $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$.
The goal word usually names the family: 'profit' → maximise; 'cost' → minimise.
Every constraint and the objective share the SAME two decision variables.

segments.text: However the problem is dressed up — sweaters or sand, calculators or crops — it is built from the same three questions. Train your eye to hunt for these three things.
Question one, what am I choosing? The unknown quantities you control become the decision variables x and y. Always write their units.
Ask it concretely. How many tables? how many hectares of land? how many scoops of powder? Whatever the problem asks you to decide, that becomes x and y.
Question two, what am I trying to make best? The total profit or total cost you want to push becomes the objective function, Z equals a x plus b y.
If it is profit or output, you push the value up and maximise. If it is cost or time or waste, you push it down and minimise.
Question three, what is stopping me? Every limit in the paragraph becomes a constraint, and each constraint is a linear inequality.
The limit could be material, money, machine time, customer demand, or a promise you made. Each separate limit is one separate constraint.
Once you hunt for these three things, every problem starts to look the same. Factory production, diet planning, transport, scheduling, they are just different costumes on one skeleton.
Before we build the procedure, four assumptions decide whether this method even applies. Know them so you can spot when a problem breaks the rules.
First, proportionality. Doubling your production must exactly double the resource you use and the profit you earn. The relationship has to be a straight line.
So watch out. If there is a bulk discount, or a one-time setup cost, the objective stops being a straight line, and the whole corner-point method no longer applies.
Second, divisibility. The graphical method happily allows fractional answers, such as x equals two point five.
In real life you cannot make half a sweater, so we round sensibly. And thankfully, C B S E problems are usually designed so the optimum lands neatly on whole numbers.
Third, hidden non-negativity. Number of buses, kilograms of fertiliser, hours worked, none of these can ever be negative.
And fourth, the big one. Read every single clause. A sentence like, type B cannot exceed type A by more than one hundred, is an entire constraint hiding in plain English.

Family one, manufacturing or product-mix. A factory makes two products from limited material or machine time. The goal is maximise profit, and its signature is resources less than or equal to what is available.

Family two, diet, nutrition, or blending. You mix two foods or feeds to meet minimum requirements cheaply. The goal is minimise cost, and its signature is nutrients greater than or equal to what is required.

Family three, transportation or allocation. You distribute goods, or split land between two uses. The goal is usually minimise cost, with a mix of supply less-than-or-equal and demand greater-than-or-equal.
Family four, scheduling or time. You divide limited hours between two activities. The goal is maximise output or earnings, with time less-than-or-equal and minimum targets greater-than-or-equal.

The shortcut is the goal word. Profit, output, or distance means maximise, and you expect less-than-or-equal constraints. Cost or requirement means minimise, and you expect greater-than-or-equal constraints.
And here is the connection back to Subtopic one. Those cost problems very often produce an unbounded region, so the half-plane verification step you learned earlier will matter.
So spot the family first. Once you know whether it is a max or a min, and which way the constraints point, half your formulation work is already done.
Let me pin down the exact symbols, especially the two phrasings that trap students every year. Treat this as your translation reference.
First, the skeleton every model shares.
You write maximise or minimise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to the structural constraints, and then, always, x and y greater than or equal to zero.
Now trap one, the difference constraint. The sentence, B cannot exceed A by more than k, where x is A and y is B.
The correct translation is y minus x less than or equal to k, which you tidy up as minus x plus y less than or equal to k.
The mistake to avoid is huge here. It does not mean y less than or equal to k. The constraint is about the gap between the two variables, not a cap on y alone.
Trap two, the multiple constraint. The sentence, A is at least twice B.
This becomes x greater than or equal to two y, or equivalently x minus two y greater than or equal to zero. Read the direction carefully, because twice multiplies the smaller quantity.
And a common cousin, B is at most one-third of A, becomes y less than or equal to one-third x, which clears to three y less than or equal to x.
Let us run the full five steps on a product-mix problem that hides a difference constraint. A printing press makes cartons of ruled notebooks and cartons of sketchbooks.
Each carton of notebooks needs one unit of paper. Each carton of sketchbooks needs two units, because the pages are thicker. Let x be notebook cartons and y sketchbook cartons.
The press has one hundred units of paper, can finish at most seventy cartons in total per day, and, because demand is limited, sketchbook cartons cannot exceed notebook cartons by more than twenty.
Profit is sixty rupees per notebook carton and one hundred forty rupees per sketchbook carton.
So the objective is maximise Z equals sixty x plus one hundred forty y.

Translating clause by clause, paper gives x plus two y less than or equal to one hundred, total output gives x plus y less than or equal to seventy, and the difference clause gives minus x plus y less than or equal to twenty, with both variables non-negative.
Plot all three lines and shade the feasible region. It is the five-cornered polygon you see on the board.

Evaluate Z at every corner. Zero comma zero gives zero, seventy comma zero gives four thousand two hundred, forty comma thirty gives six thousand six hundred, twenty comma forty gives six thousand eight hundred, and zero comma twenty gives two thousand eight hundred.

The maximum is six thousand eight hundred at twenty comma forty. Notice the winning point sits exactly where the difference clause, minus x plus y equals twenty, is active. That is the very clause a careless reader would have dropped.

This becomes x greater than or equal to two y, or equivalently x minus two y greater than or equal to zero. Read the direction carefully, because twice multiplies the smaller quantity.
And a common cousin, B is at most one-third of A, becomes y less than or equal to one-third x, which clears to three y less than or equal to x.
Let us run the full five steps on a product-mix problem that hides a difference constraint. A printing press makes cartons of ruled notebooks and cartons of sketchbooks.
Each carton of notebooks needs one unit of paper. Each carton of sketchbooks needs two units, because the pages are thicker. Let x be notebook cartons and y sketchbook cartons.
The press has one hundred units of paper, can finish at most seventy cartons in total per day, and, because demand is limited, sketchbook cartons cannot exceed notebook cartons by more than twenty.
Profit is sixty rupees per notebook carton and one hundred forty rupees per sketchbook carton.
So the objective is maximise Z equals sixty x plus one hundred forty y.

Translating clause by clause, paper gives x plus two y less than or equal to one hundred, total output gives x plus y less than or equal to seventy, and the difference clause gives minus x plus y less than or equal to twenty, with both variables non-negative.
Plot all three lines and shade the feasible region. It is the five-cornered polygon you see on the board.

Evaluate Z at every corner. Zero comma zero gives zero, seventy comma zero gives four thousand two hundred, forty comma thirty gives six thousand six hundred, twenty comma forty gives six thousand eight hundred, and zero comma twenty gives two thousand eight hundred.

The maximum is six thousand eight hundred at twenty comma forty. Notice the winning point sits exactly where the difference clause, minus x plus y equals twenty, is active. That is the very clause a careless reader would have dropped.

Four ways a Linear Programming problem can end
So far every LPP behaved nicely: one region, one clean optimal corner. Real problems don't always cooperate.
1. One clear highest spot — a unique optimal solution (the usual, happy case).
2. A whole ridge at the same height — multiple optimal solutions.
3. The field never ends uphill — an unbounded solution; no highest point exists.
4. There is no field at all — no feasible solution; the constraints contradict.

segments.text: Now a higher-order allocation problem where three constraints all bite at once. A farmer has twelve hectares to split between wheat and mustard.
Let x be hectares of wheat and y hectares of mustard. The land itself is capped at twelve hectares.

Wheat needs two person-days of labour per hectare, mustard needs one, and only eighteen are available. Wheat needs one unit of water per hectare, mustard needs three, and only twenty four are available.
Expected profit is five thousand rupees per hectare of wheat and four thousand per hectare of mustard, so we maximise Z equals five thousand x plus four thousand y.

The three limits become x plus y less than or equal to twelve for land, two x plus y less than or equal to eighteen for labour, and x plus three y less than or equal to twenty four for water, with both variables non-negative.
Plot the three lines. Something special happens here, which the board makes clear. All three lines pass through one single vertex.
Evaluate the corners. Zero comma zero gives zero, nine comma zero gives forty five thousand, six comma six gives fifty four thousand, and zero comma eight gives thirty two thousand.

The twist is at six comma six. There, all three constraints hold as equalities. Land is six plus six, that is twelve. Labour is twelve plus six, that is eighteen. Water is six plus eighteen, that is twenty four. Every resource is fully used.

So the maximum profit is fifty four thousand rupees. Plant six hectares of wheat and six of mustard. This is exactly why you must check every corner, because the winner is where the binding constraints intersect.
Here is a pure translation drill with a mixed bag of phrasings. A student earns from two freelance gigs, data-entry and graphic design, in hours per week.
Let x be data-entry hours and y be graphic-design hours per week.
Clause one, she has at most twenty working hours a week. At most means less-than-or-equal, so x plus y less than or equal to twenty. This is a capacity constraint.
Clause two, her client caps data-entry at twelve hours. That is an upper bound on a single variable, x less than or equal to twelve.
Clause three, to build her portfolio she wants at least five hours of design. At least means greater-than-or-equal, so y greater than or equal to five. This is a requirement.
Data-entry pays one hundred fifty rupees an hour and design two hundred fifty, and she wants maximum earnings, so maximise Z equals one hundred fifty x plus two hundred fifty y.
Plot the four lines. Notice that y greater than or equal to five already forces y positive, so a separate y greater than or equal to zero is redundant but harmless.
The region is bounded, because the total-hours cap of twenty closes it off. So by Theorem two, both a maximum and a minimum exist at corner points, and it is ready for the graphical method.

The lesson is the payoff of clause-by-clause work. A single messy sentence full of at most, at least, and capped at becomes four clean lines, one per clause, once you translate each phrase separately.
Until now every problem we solved behaved beautifully. One feasible region, one clean optimal corner. But real problems, and exam problems designed to test you, do not always cooperate.
Think of solving an L P P as searching a fenced field for the highest point your ruler reads. Exactly four things can happen, and a complete student recognises all four on sight.
Outcome one, there is one clear highest spot. This is the unique optimal solution, the usual, happy case we have seen all along.
Outcome two, there is a whole ridge at the same height. Your ruler lies flat along one fence, so every point on that fence ties for best. These are multiple optimal solutions.
Outcome three, the field never ends in the uphill direction. You can keep walking and keep climbing forever, so there is no highest point. That is an unbounded solution.
Outcome four, there is no field at all. The fences contradict each other so badly that no point satisfies them all. The region is empty, and the problem has no answer.
The board shows all four side by side. Learn to picture each one, because naming the outcome quickly is the whole skill of this subtopic.

Here is the vivid version of outcome four. A shopkeeper insists, I must sell at least sixty items today, but also, my shelf holds at most forty items. No honest number can satisfy both. That is an infeasible problem.

board_events.text: Many unbounded regions still give a perfectly good minimum — every cost-diet problem does.
'Region unbounded' describes geometry; 'solution unbounded' describes the answer. Never confuse them.
A maximum fails only when the region is unbounded in the direction $Z$ increases.
If the region is bounded, Theorem 2 guarantees both a max and a min — no special case can arise.
Each outcome and its tell-tale sign on the graph
Unique optimum: the objective line touches the region last at a single corner.
Multiple optima: two corners tie; the objective line is parallel to the edge joining them.
Unbounded solution: the region is unbounded and 'better than every corner' still overlaps it.
No feasible solution: the constraints share no common shaded region — the region is empty.
Redundant constraint: a line you can remove without changing the region at all.
Its line lies entirely outside, or along the far edge of, the region formed by the others.
Read the picture well and you can name the outcome before computing a single value.
The properties, stated precisely
Multiple optima: if $Z$ is optimal at two corners, it is optimal at every point on the joining segment.

board_events.latex: Z(\text{corner}_1) = Z(\text{corner}_2) \;\Rightarrow\; \text{the whole joining edge is optimal}

board_events.text: Unbounded max test: for the largest corner value $M$, the maximum fails if $ax + by \gt M$ meets the region.
Infeasibility: if the intersection of all constraint half-planes (with $x, y \ge 0$) is empty, there is no solution.
Redundancy: removing a redundant constraint leaves the region — and the optimum — unchanged.
A bounded region can NEVER be infeasible or unbounded — Theorem 2 rules both out.
So the first thing to settle is always: does a common region exist, and is it bounded?

segments.text: Before the worked cases, burn one distinction into memory, because it is the single most common confusion in this chapter.
An unbounded region means the shape of the feasible set stretches off to infinity. That is a statement about geometry, about the picture.
An unbounded solution means the objective function has no finite optimum. That is a statement about the answer, about the value of Z.

The board makes the gap obvious. Here is one unbounded region. It clearly has a genuine minimum at the marked corner, yet the objective grows without limit in the up-right direction, so it has no maximum.
This is the everyday situation, not an exception. Many unbounded regions still yield a perfectly good minimum. Every cost-minimisation diet problem you formulated in Subtopic two is exactly this.
So keep the words separate. Region unbounded describes the geometry. Solution unbounded describes the answer. A region can be unbounded and still hand you a finite minimum.
When does a maximum actually fail? Only when the region is unbounded in the very direction that Z increases. If it opens the other way, the maximum can still exist.
And the clean guarantee. If the region is bounded, Theorem two promises both a maximum and a minimum, each at a corner. No special case can arise in a bounded region at all.
Each of the four outcomes leaves a distinct fingerprint on the graph. Learn the fingerprints and you diagnose the problem at a glance.
For a unique optimum, the objective line, as it slides outward, touches the region for the last time at a single corner. One clean winner.
For multiple optima, two corners tie for the best value, and the tell-tale sign is that the objective line runs exactly parallel to the edge joining those two corners.
For an unbounded solution, the region is unbounded, and the open half-plane meaning better than every corner still overlaps the region. There is always a feasible point that beats your best vertex.
For no feasible solution, the constraints share no common shaded region at all. When you shade everything, nothing is left over. The feasible region is empty.
There is also a fifth thing worth naming, a redundant constraint. This is a line you could remove entirely without changing the region.
You spot it because its line lies completely outside the region, or lies along the far edge, never actually forming a boundary that the other constraints have not already set.
The payoff is speed. Read the picture carefully and you can name the outcome, unique, multiple, unbounded, or infeasible, before you compute a single value of Z.
Now the same four ideas stated as precise properties, the kind an examiner wants written down.
First, multiple optima. If Z attains its optimum at two corner points, then it attains that same value at every point on the segment joining them, giving infinitely many optimal solutions.
In symbols, when Z at corner one equals Z at corner two, the whole edge joining them is optimal.

Second, the unbounded maximum test. For a maximisation problem on an unbounded region with largest corner value big M, the maximum fails to exist if the open half-plane a x plus b y greater than big M has any point in common with the region.

Third, infeasibility. If the intersection of all the constraint half-planes, including x and y greater than or equal to zero, is the empty set, then the L P P has no feasible solution, and hence no optimal solution.
Fourth, redundancy. Removing a redundant constraint leaves the feasible region, and therefore the optimal solution, completely unchanged.
And the master fact that governs all of them. A bounded region can never be infeasible and never be unbounded. Theorem two rules out both special cases at once.
Which is why the very first thing to settle in any special-case question is this. Does a common region even exist, and if it does, is it bounded?

sections.title: Detection procedures and a five-second triage & related topics

board_events.text: Detection procedures — spotting each case while solving
No feasible solution: plot all constraints; if no region is common to all, stop — 'no feasible solution'.
Unbounded solution: confirm the region is unbounded, find largest corner $M$, then test $ax + by \gt M$.
If that half-plane meets the region, write '$Z$ has no maximum' — but a minimum may still exist.
Multiple optima: evaluate $Z$ at all corners; if two tie, the whole joining segment is optimal.
Redundant constraint: if removing a line leaves the region unchanged, that constraint is redundant.
Run this as a triage BEFORE grinding through corners — it saves time and prevents classic errors.
5-second triage: common region? (else infeasible) → bounded? (if yes, both exist) → else verify.
Worked example — no feasible solution
A coaching centre runs $x$ morning and $y$ evening batches, maximising enrolment $Z = 30x + 25y$.
Staff: at least 6 morning and at least 6 evening. Rooms: at most 10 batches total per day.

segments.text: Here is how you actively detect each case while you are solving, rather than being surprised by it at the end.

To detect no feasible solution, plot and shade every constraint as usual, then look for a region common to all of them in the first quadrant. If no such common region exists, stop and write, the L P P has no feasible solution.

To detect an unbounded solution, first confirm the region is unbounded, then evaluate Z at all corner points and call the largest value big M, and finally test the open half-plane a x plus b y greater than big M.

If that half-plane shares any point with the region, then the objective can exceed big M, so you write, Z has no maximum. But remember, the same region may still have a perfectly valid minimum, so check that separately.
To detect multiple optima, evaluate Z at all corners, and if the optimum value is attained at two of them, then every point on the segment between them is also optimal.
To detect a redundant constraint, draw the region using all constraints, and if removing one line leaves the region unchanged because that line never forms a boundary, that constraint is redundant.
The smart move is to run all of this as a quick triage before you grind through the corner-point table. It saves time and prevents the classic special-case slips.

The triage is only five seconds. Is there a common region? If not, infeasible. Is it bounded? If yes, both a max and a min exist and there is no special case. Only if it is unbounded do you need the verification test.
Let us see infeasibility on a concrete problem. A coaching centre wants to run x morning batches and y evening batches, and it hopes to maximise total enrolment, Z equals thirty x plus twenty five y.
The staffing promise says it must run at least six morning and at least six evening batches. The room capacity says it can run at most ten batches in total per day.
So the constraints are x greater than or equal to six, y greater than or equal to six, and x plus y less than or equal to ten, with both variables non-negative.
Now look at the tension. The first two constraints together force x plus y to be at least six plus six, that is at least twelve.
But the room constraint demands x plus y at most ten. So we need x plus y to be both at least twelve and at most ten, which is impossible.
The board shows it geometrically. The block where x and y are each at least six sits in the upper right, and the triangle where x plus y is at most ten sits in the lower left. They never touch.
So no pair x, y can satisfy both x plus y at least twelve and x plus y at most ten at the same time. The shaded regions simply do not overlap.

Therefore the feasible region is empty. The L P P has no feasible solution, and there is no optimal value of Z. The interpretation is that the staffing promise and the room capacity are in conflict, and one of them must be relaxed.

Now the textbook trap, an unbounded region with no maximum but a perfectly good minimum. We maximise Z equals five x plus four y, subject to x plus y greater than or equal to eight, with both variables non-negative.
The problem is stated compactly, but read the constraints carefully.
There are only greater-than-or-equal and non-negativity constraints, so the region lies above the line x plus y equals eight and stretches away to infinity up and to the right. It is unbounded.
Find the boundary corners. At eight comma zero, Z is forty. At zero comma eight, Z is thirty two. So the largest corner value, big M, is forty.
A hurried student would stop and write forty. But the region is unbounded, so we must test whether we can beat it, and the board shows the answer visually.

Test the half-plane five x plus four y greater than forty. Take the feasible point twenty comma zero, since twenty is at least eight. There Z equals one hundred, which is greater than forty. A feasible point beats the best corner, so there is no maximum.
And we can push as far as we like. At one hundred comma zero, Z equals five hundred, and it keeps climbing without any limit at all.

But do not over-correct. This very same region does have a minimum. Z equals thirty two at zero comma eight, and this is verified because five x plus four y less than thirty two misses the region entirely. Unbounded region, no maximum, but a genuine minimum.

problem chhote mein di hai, par constraints dhyan se padhiye.

board_events.text: $x \le 12$ is redundant: its line never forms a boundary of the region.
Removing it leaves the region — and the optimum of any linear objective — completely unchanged.
Lesson: not every line you're given actually shapes the region. Check which ones truly form the boundary.
Special-case pitfalls and a 5-second triage
Pitfall 1 — 'unbounded region' ⇒ 'no answer'. Wrong: most cost problems have a valid minimum.
Always run the half-plane test before declaring 'no optimum'.
Pitfall 2 — counting multiple optima as 'two'. A tie means infinitely many (the whole edge).
Pitfall 3 — missing infeasibility. If no common region exists, don't force corners — state it plainly.
Pitfall 4 — treating every constraint as binding. Some are redundant; check which form the boundary.
Triage: common region? (else infeasible) → bounded? (if yes both exist) → only if unbounded, verify.
This quick classification saves time and prevents every classic special-case error.

segments.text: Now a clean case of multiple optimal solutions. We maximise Z equals two x plus two y, subject to x plus y less than or equal to six, x less than or equal to four, y less than or equal to four, and both variables non-negative.
This region is bounded, so by Theorem two a maximum certainly exists. The question is how many optimal points there are.
List the corners. They are zero comma zero, four comma zero, four comma two, two comma four, and zero comma four.
Evaluate Z at each. The interesting ones are four comma two, which gives twelve, and two comma four, which also gives twelve. The maximum value twelve is reached at two corners at once.
The board shows why. Both of those corners lie on the line x plus y equals six, and the objective line runs exactly parallel to that edge.
So by the multiple-optima property, when Z ties at two corners, every single point on the segment joining them, which here lies along x plus y equals six, also gives Z equals twelve.
That means there are infinitely many optimal solutions, not just two. The answer is the whole edge between four comma two and two comma four.
And the reason is geometric. The objective line two x plus two y equals twelve is exactly parallel to that edge, so the ruler lies flat along it and every point reads the same best value.

The last special case is the redundant constraint. A feasible region is defined by x plus y less than or equal to ten, x less than or equal to twelve, and both variables non-negative. Which constraint is redundant?
Focus on the two upper limits and reason about them together in the first quadrant.
Within the first quadrant, the constraint x plus y less than or equal to ten already forces x to be at most ten, because y cannot be negative.

So the constraint x less than or equal to twelve can never actually bind. Every point that the other constraints allow automatically satisfies x less than or equal to twelve, since x is already at most ten.
The board makes it visible. The line x equals twelve sits well to the right of the whole region, never touching it.
Therefore x less than or equal to twelve is redundant. Its line never forms a boundary of the region, because the paper-and-quadrant constraints already do its job and more.
Removing it leaves the region unchanged, and therefore leaves the optimum of any linear objective over that region completely unchanged too.
The lesson is a useful habit. Not every line you are handed actually shapes the region. Before you solve, always check which constraints truly form the boundary and which are just along for the ride.
Let me close the special cases with the four traps students fall into, and the quick triage that beats all of them.
Pitfall one, believing that an unbounded region means no answer. That is simply wrong. Most cost-minimisation problems have an unbounded region and a perfectly valid minimum.
So the rule is firm. Always run the half-plane test before you ever declare that there is no optimum.
Pitfall two, counting multiple optima as just two. A tie at two corners does not mean two answers. It means infinitely many, because the whole edge between them is optimal.
Pitfall three, missing infeasibility. If you cannot find a common shaded region, do not force yourself to invent corner points. State plainly that there is no feasible solution.
Pitfall four, treating every constraint as binding. Some constraints are redundant and never touch the region. Check which lines actually form the boundary before you solve.

And here is the triage that prevents all four. First, is there a common region? If not, it is infeasible. Second, is it bounded? If yes, both a max and a min exist and there is no special case. Only if it is unbounded do you need the verification test.
This five-second classification, done before you grind any numbers, saves time and prevents every one of the classic special-case errors.

board_events.text: Formulation: turning a paragraph into mathematics
In an exam nobody hands you the inequalities — they hand you a paragraph.
Opener: 'A tailoring unit has 40 metres of cloth and 18 hours of machine time…'
The hardest, most marks-rich skill here is turning those words into a model.
Think of yourself as a translator at a railway enquiry counter.
The passenger speaks everyday language; you convert it into the system's exact codes.
'We can't afford more than ₹5000' becomes the exact symbol: cost ≤ 5000.
Get one word wrong — 'at least' read as 'at most' — and the whole answer collapses.
The five-step formulation procedure
Step 1 — Name the decision variables, with units: '$x$ = number of cricket bats'.
Step 2 — Write the objective $Z = (\text{rate}_x)\,x + (\text{rate}_y)\,y$; state max or min.
Step 3 — Translate each restriction clause-by-clause into a linear inequality.
Working clause by clause means you never miss a hidden constraint.
Step 4 — Add non-negativity $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$ (this also fences the region into quadrant I).
Step 5 — State the complete model: 'Maximise $Z = \dots$ subject to $\dots$'.

Formulation pitfalls and a 10-second sanity scan
Pitfall 1 — reversing ≤ and ≥. 'At least' is ≥; 'at most' is ≤. Underline the limiting words first.
Pitfall 2 — dropping a hidden constraint. 'B cannot exceed A by more than 100' is a full constraint.
Work clause by clause so no restriction escapes.
Pitfall 3 — forgetting non-negativity. Examiners deduct marks for a missing $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$.

(iii) is non-negativity present? (iv) do cost/'at least' carry ≥ and profit/'at most' carry ≤?

Cheat sheet — one-screen revision
Objective $Z = ax + by$; constraints are linear inequalities plus non-negativity $x, y \ge 0$.
Corner-Point Method: draw region → list ALL vertices → tabulate $Z$ → pick best (verify if unbounded).
Bounded ⇒ both max & min exist. Unbounded ⇒ verify, or the optimum may vanish.
Translate words: 'at most / available' → ≤; 'at least / requires' → ≥; 'uses all / exactly' → =.
Four families: product-mix (max, ≤) · diet (min, ≥) · transport (≤ & ≥) · scheduling (time ≤, target ≥).

segments.text: In Subtopic one you learned how to solve a Linear Programming problem once it is written in clean mathematical form. Now we tackle the harder half.
Because in a real exam, and in real life, nobody hands you the inequalities ready-made. They hand you a paragraph of ordinary language.
Something like, a tailoring unit has forty metres of cloth and eighteen hours of machine time, and so on. Your first job is to convert that story into mathematics.
That conversion is called formulation, and it is the hardest and most marks-rich skill in this whole chapter. Get it right and everything after is mechanical.
Here is the mindset. Think of yourself as a translator sitting at a railway enquiry counter.
A passenger speaks to you in everyday Hindi or Tamil, and you must convert their request into the precise codes the booking system understands.
Formulation is exactly that translation. The loose sentence, we cannot afford more than five thousand rupees, becomes the exact symbol, cost less than or equal to five thousand.
And here is the warning that runs through this subtopic. Get one single word wrong, read at least as at most, and the entire answer collapses, no matter how perfectly you draw the graph afterwards.
Formulation is a procedure, not a theorem, so here is the disciplined five-step framework. Follow it in order every time.

Step one, name the decision variables and write their units. For example, let x equal the number of cricket bats and y the number of tennis racquets. Stating units now stops you mixing hours with items later.

Step two, write the objective function. Find the per-unit profit or cost of each variable and combine, Z equals rate for x times x plus rate for y times y. Say clearly whether you maximise or minimise.
Step three, translate each restriction. Go through the paragraph one sentence at a time, and for each limit write a linear inequality using the dictionary to fix the direction of the sign.
Working clause by clause is the whole discipline. It is the only reliable way to make sure no hidden constraint slips past you.
Step four, add non-negativity, x and y greater than or equal to zero. This is physically obvious, and it also fences the whole region into the first quadrant.
Step five, state the complete model together, maximise Z equals something subject to the full list of constraints. A clean, collected model is what earns the formulation marks.
The board shows the journey. A word problem goes through the five-step formulation into an L P P model, then through the corner-point method into the optimal solution.
One memory hook to carry the whole procedure. N O C N. Name the variables, write the Objective, list the Constraints, add Non-negativity.
This one asks only for the model, which is perfect for drilling the diet family. A fitness coach blends two protein powders, P and Q, measured in scoops.
One scoop of P gives twelve grams of protein and twenty grams of carbohydrate. One scoop of Q gives eight grams of protein and thirty grams of carbohydrate. Let x be scoops of P and y scoops of Q.
The client needs at least forty eight grams of protein and at least one hundred twenty grams of carbohydrate per day. P costs fifteen rupees a scoop and Q costs ten.
Because this is a cost problem, the objective is minimise Z equals fifteen x plus ten y.
The protein requirement is twelve x plus eight y greater than or equal to forty eight, and dividing through by four tidies it to three x plus two y greater than or equal to twelve.
The carbohydrate requirement is twenty x plus thirty y greater than or equal to one hundred twenty, and dividing by ten gives two x plus three y greater than or equal to twelve.
Sketch the region. Because both constraints are greater-than-or-equal, the region sits above both lines and opens out to infinity. It is unbounded.

That is the whole point of recognising the family early. Diet means minimise, which means greater-than-or-equal constraints, which means an unbounded region, which means you must run the half-plane verification when you go on to solve.

The question asked for formulation only, so the model is complete. Minimise Z equals fifteen x plus ten y, subject to three x plus two y greater than or equal to twelve, two x plus three y greater than or equal to twelve, and both variables non-negative.
Let me close Part two with the four formulation slips that cost marks, and a ten-second scan that catches almost all of them.

Pitfall one, reversing the inequality. At least is greater-than-or-equal, at most is less-than-or-equal. A single flip turns a sensible answer into nonsense, so underline the limiting words before writing any symbol.
Pitfall two, dropping a hidden constraint. Sentences like B cannot exceed A by more than one hundred, or must produce at least ten of B, are full constraints in disguise.
The cure is the same discipline as before. Work through the paragraph clause by clause, so not a single restriction escapes you.

Pitfall three, forgetting non-negativity. Items, hours, kilograms, hectares, none can be negative. Examiners deduct marks for a missing x and y greater than or equal to zero, even if everything else is perfect.

Pitfall four, choosing the wrong decision variables. If you cannot write the objective and every constraint using just your two variables, you picked them badly. Re-read the question and take whatever it asks you to decide.
And here is the ten-second sanity scan to run after every formulation. First, does the objective say max or min to match the goal word? Second, is there one constraint for each limiting sentence?

Third, is non-negativity present? And fourth, do the cost and at-least problems carry greater-than-or-equal, while the profit and at-most problems carry less-than-or-equal? If all four check out, your model is almost certainly right.

Before the final revision card, here is your complete Linear Programming toolkit, gathered in one place. This section restates, it does not re-teach, so treat it as the sheet you glance at before the exam.
At the centre of everything is the objective function, Z equals a x plus b y.
First, the profit family, written as a maximisation.
Maximise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to each resource constraint c i x plus d i y less than or equal to e i, together with x and y greater than or equal to zero.
Second, the cost family, written as a minimisation.
Minimise Z equals a x plus b y, subject to each requirement c i x plus d i y greater than or equal to e i, again with x and y greater than or equal to zero.
Hold the two theorems firmly. Theorem one, the optimum sits at a corner. Theorem two, a bounded region guarantees both a maximum and a minimum, while an unbounded region may or may not have either.

And the two verification lines for unbounded regions. There is no maximum if a x plus b y greater than big M still meets the region, and no minimum if a x plus b y less than small m still meets the region.
Finally, keep the two trap translations at your fingertips. Minus x plus y less than or equal to k means B exceeds A by at most k, and x greater than or equal to two y means A is at least twice B.
And finally, the one-screen cheat sheet. Everything in this chapter, compressed to what you can scan in the last minute before the paper.

That conversion is called formulation, and it is the hardest and most marks-rich skill in this whole chapter. Get it right and everything after is mechanical.
